_note: Decisions X-012 and X-015 (docs/audit/DECISIONS.md). Named views of truth and of ethics, and real thinkers who held them. Each thinker's summary must match their documented views and cite a source. Advisor lines are written for the game in the thinker's way of reasoning; they are not quotations and are labelled as imagined. Add thinkers from many traditions.

views.name: Correspondence theory of truth
views.plain: A claim is true when it matches how things really are.

views.name: Coherence theory of truth
views.plain: A claim is true when it fits together with everything else we have good reason to believe.

views.name: Pragmatic theory of truth
views.plain: A claim is true when it works: it holds up when we act on it and test it over time.

views.name: Virtue ethics
views.plain: Ask what a good person would do. Good actions come from good character, built by practice.

views.name: Duty ethics (deontology)
views.plain: Some actions are right or wrong in themselves. Act only in a way you could want everyone to act.

views.name: Consequentialism
views.plain: Judge an action by its results: choose what brings the most benefit and the least harm to everyone affected.

views.name: Ethics of care
views.plain: Start from relationships. Ask who depends on whom, and how to respond to their real needs.

views.name: Ubuntu
views.plain: A person is a person through other persons. Ask what keeps the community whole.

thinkers.name: Aristotle
thinkers.summary: In the Metaphysics, Aristotle says that to say of what is that it is, and of what is not that it is not, is true. In the Nicomachean Ethics, he says that virtues are habits of character built by practice.

source.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Ethics

advice.correspondence: Look at the thing itself. Does your claim say of what is, that it is? If the object and the claim do not match, change the claim.
advice.virtue: Do not look only for a rule. Ask what an honest and careful person would do here, then do that until it becomes a habit.

thinkers.name: Bertrand Russell
thinkers.summary: In The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Russell argues that a belief is true when it corresponds to a fact, and false when there is no such fact.

source.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Correspondence Theory of Truth

advice.correspondence: Which fact would make this claim true? Name it. Then go and find out whether that fact is there.

thinkers.name: Baruch Spinoza
thinkers.place: Amsterdam and The Hague, Dutch Republic
thinkers.summary: Spinoza built his Ethics (1677) as one connected system, in which each idea follows from others. Historians of philosophy often name him among the early thinkers linked to the coherence theory.

source.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Coherence Theory of Truth

advice.coherence: Set this idea beside the others you trust. Does it follow from them, or does it pull against them? An idea that fits nothing needs more care.

thinkers.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
thinkers.place: Stuttgart and Berlin, in present-day Germany
thinkers.summary: Hegel wrote that the true is the whole. He held that a single claim gets its full meaning only inside a developing system of knowledge.

source.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Coherence Theory of Truth

advice.coherence: One record alone is only a part. Put it with the ledger, the song and the object. What picture does the whole make, and where does a part not fit?

thinkers.name: William James
thinkers.place: New York and Massachusetts, United States
thinkers.summary: In Pragmatism (1907), James argues that true ideas are those we can take in, check and confirm, and that truth shows itself in what an idea does for us over time.

advice.pragmatic: What difference would it make if this claim were true? Act on it in a small way, and see whether it holds up.

thinkers.name: Charles Sanders Peirce
thinkers.summary: Peirce described truth as the opinion that careful inquiry would finally agree on, if it went on long enough.

advice.pragmatic: Do not stop at the first answer. Ask what more checking would show, and who else should check it with you.

thinkers.name: Ibn al-Haytham
thinkers.summary: In his Book of Optics, Ibn al-Haytham tested claims about light and sight with careful, repeatable experiments. He wrote that a seeker of truth must test the claims of famous books, and must also doubt his own judgement.

source.title: Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers: Ibn al-Haytham

advice.correspondence: Do not trust a claim because a famous book says it. Find a test that anyone can repeat, and check whether the world agrees.

thinkers.name: Ibn Khaldun
thinkers.summary: In the Muqaddimah, the introduction to his history, Ibn Khaldun warned that historians copy reports without testing them. He tested each report against what is possible in human society: how people live, eat, travel and govern.

advice.coherence: Do not judge a report by who wrote it. Ask whether it fits everything else you know about how people really live.

thinkers.name: Mozi
thinkers.place: the state of Lu or Song, in present-day China
thinkers.summary: The Mohist writings give three tests for a claim: its basis in the deeds of the past, what ordinary people have seen and heard, and its benefit when put into use. Mohists judged actions by the benefit they bring to all.

advice.pragmatic: Use three tests. What did people in the past find? What have ordinary people seen and heard? What happens when you put it into use?
advice.consequences: Count everyone this choice touches, not only the people in front of you. Which choice brings the most benefit to all of them?

thinkers.name: Kongzi (Confucius)
thinkers.place: the state of Lu, in present-day China
thinkers.summary: The Analects, compiled by his followers, describe the exemplary person (junzi), who practises humaneness (ren) and right conduct in relationships. Many scholars compare this with virtue ethics.

advice.virtue: How would an exemplary person treat the people in this choice: the elder, the stranger, the friend? Begin with your own conduct.

thinkers.name: Immanuel Kant
thinkers.summary: In the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785), Kant argues that we should act only on a rule that we could will to be a universal law, and treat people never only as a means.

source.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Moral Philosophy

advice.duty: Could everyone act on the rule you are about to follow? If everyone did, would the rule still work? Do not use a person only as a tool.

thinkers.name: John Stuart Mill
thinkers.summary: In Utilitarianism (1861), Mill argues that actions are right as they tend to promote happiness and wrong as they tend to produce the opposite.

advice.consequences: Who will be happier, and who will be harmed, if you choose this? Count each person's good the same.

thinkers.name: Nel Noddings
thinkers.place: New Jersey and California, United States
thinkers.summary: In Caring (1984), Noddings describes ethics as starting in caring relations: paying close attention to another person and responding to what they need.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Care Ethics

advice.care: Who is waiting on this choice? Listen to what they actually need, not what you guess they need. Then respond to them.

thinkers.name: Desmond Tutu
thinkers.place: Klerksdorp and Cape Town, South Africa
thinkers.summary: In No Future Without Forgiveness (1999), Tutu describes ubuntu, an idea from Nguni-speaking peoples such as the Xhosa and Zulu: a person is a person through other persons, so harm to one diminishes all.

source.title: Desmond Tutu, No Future Without Forgiveness (1999)

advice.ubuntu: Which choice keeps this community whole? If one person is shamed or left out, ask what that does to everyone else here.
